newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Upper House set to abandon Bonn for Berlin.
newsitem.headline: German Upper House set to abandon Bonn for Berlin.

text.p: Germany's upper house of parliament is set to reverse its earlier decision to remain in Bonn and instead vote on Friday to join the government and lower house when they move to Berlin later this decade.

The Bundesrat, or upper house, had narrowly elected to stay in Bonn five years ago after the 672-member lower house voted to move the seat of government to Berlin, the German capital until the end of World War Two.

But a growing number of Bundesrat members, who represent Germany's 16 federal states, have complained that the upper house would lose influence if it were to stay behind in Bonn, 600 km (375 miles) west of Berlin.

They argue it would also be a waste of money if officials had to shuttle between the two legislative chambers hundreds of miles (km) apart. Thirteen of the 16 states are expected to back the proposal on Friday to move to Berlin.

Even Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who has supported efforts to keep some federal ministries in Bonn, has called the Bundesrat's 1991 decision to stay behind after the rest of the government moves to Berlin absurd.
The government plans to move from Bonn, a quiet Rhineside town of 300,000 that was West Germany's provisional capital between 1949 and 1990, to the 3.4 million metropolis in 1999.
"The importance of the Bundesrat would be reduced if it were to stay in Bonn," Edmund Stoiber, premier of Bavaria state, wrote in a commentary for the Bonn daily General-Anzeiger.
The upper house's expected decision on Friday in favour of Berlin will likely bring new momentum to the oft-delayed and still controversial plans to move to Berlin.
Now, Berlin, which had astutely reserved the old Prussian House of Lords building near the central Potsdamer Platz square for the Bundesrat, may celebrate another victory over Bonn.
"The Bundesrat's (expected) decision will lead to the loss off 1,000 jobs in Bonn," said Bonn mayor Baerbel Dieckmann. "The Bundesrat will be breaking its promise."
Despite the exodus to Berlin, seven of the government's 16 ministries, including defence and health, will stay in Bonn to help cushion the economic blow for the city.
About 18,500 government officials, mostly in the upper levels of the bureaucracy, will be moving to Berlin.
The Bundesrat meets once per month and has a relatively small staff of 200.
